European Train Guide

Every train operator in Europe and what each one actually runs — high-speed, intercity, regional, night trains, private operators, rail passes and scenic lines. For each: the country it is based in, the countries it crosses and the stops it serves. Search by operator, country, city or route, or filter by the type of train you need. It answers the question that comes before booking: who runs this line, and is it the fast one.

The spine

where high-speed crosses a border

The one continent where rail is a network. The eleven country sections below are unchanged — this is the summary that points into them.

🇬🇧Channel TunnelLondon – Paris / Brussels / Amsterdam2h 16mEurostar, now including the old Thalys network.
🇮🇹The Italian spineTurin – Milan – Florence – Rome – Naples~4h 30mTrenitalia and Italo run the same track. Compare both.
🇪🇸Madrid – BarcelonaAVE, Iryo and OUIGO on one line2h 30mThree operators competing. Never book the first fare you see.
🇩🇪The German networkFrankfurt – Berlin / Hamburg / Munich~4hICE, with FlixTrain undercutting it on the big routes.
🇦🇹The night networkVienna – Hamburg / Amsterdam, Brussels – PragueovernightNightjet and European Sleeper. Book the moment they open.
Seven open-access operators undercut the incumbent — Italo, Iryo, FlixTrain, Lumo, RegioJet, Westbahn and GoVolta. On a big route, check both. Rail passes have their own page — Rail Passes & Tickets compares every pass worth buying.

What it is like

Fast, civilised and priced like an airline — book months ahead or pay dearly, because walk-up fares are brutal. Treat it as a flight at the London end: check-in closes 30–45 minutes before departure and there is airport-style security and passport control. Standard Premier buys a wider seat and a tray of food rather than a different class of travel; the Thalys merger means one booking system and one loyalty scheme across the old network.

What it is like

The best night train in Europe and the reason the whole category came back. The new-generation cars carry single mini-cabins, which finally makes a solo sleeper affordable; couchettes are the value pick and the private sleeper compartments are the ones that sell out first. Book the moment the window opens — popular runs like Vienna–Paris and Zurich–Amsterdam go months ahead.

What it is like

Worth supporting and worth riding if the route suits you, but do not book a tight onward connection off the back of it.

Eurail / Interrail Pass
Not an operator — multi-country rail pass
Rail Pass
Coverage
33 European countries
ℹ
How It Works Valid on most national railways across Europe. Eurail for non-EU residents; Interrail for EU/EEA residents. Reservations often required separately (especially high-speed + night trains) — the newer Plus Pass bundles most seat reservations into the price. Passes are now app-only via the Rail Planner app (paper passes retired).
What it is like

The pass only pays if you are moving often and moving far. The trap is reservations: they are compulsory and separately charged on almost everything in France, Spain and Italy, so a pass there buys less freedom than it appears to. Where it shines is Germany, Austria, Switzerland and central Europe, where you can walk onto most trains with nothing but the pass.

What it is like

France's high-speed backbone, and it works — city centre to city centre at 300 km/h with a compulsory reservation, so there is no such thing as turning up and boarding. Prices climb steeply as the train fills, so the same seat can triple in a fortnight. Second class is perfectly comfortable; first buys quiet and elbow room rather than service.

What it is like

The low-cost sibling, and it behaves like one: cabin-bag limits with real fees for anything larger, no catering, and some services using outlying stations rather than the central terminus. Check which Paris station you are actually leaving from before congratulating yourself on the fare. Booked early for a simple A-to-B run it is exceptional value.

What it is like

Bare-bones and inexpensive — six-berth couchettes, thin blankets, and an early arrival whether you are ready or not. The four-berth option and the women-only compartments are both worth requesting. It is the cheapest way to reach the Alps or the Pyrenees from Paris without losing a day, and nobody rides it for the comfort.

What it is like

The network is superb on paper and the punctuality no longer matches it — long-distance ICE delays are common enough that DB publishes the statistics and they make uncomfortable reading. Buy the Sparpreis fare early and accept it is train-specific; Flexpreis costs far more but lets you take the next service when yours is late, which on this railway is a real feature. Reserve a seat on any busy corridor.

Cheap, cheerful and thin on the ground — a couple of departures a day on a handful of routes, in stock that is comfortable enough without pretending to be anything more. What it is like

Frecciarossa 1000 does Milan–Rome in about three hours and is the best way to travel the length of Italy. Two things catch visitors: regional tickets must be validated before boarding, and national rail strikes are frequent, announced in advance, and always preserve a guaranteed minimum service — check the date before you book. Business class is a modest premium and often worth it.

The private competitor on Italy's high-speed lines, usually a little cheaper than Trenitalia for the same journey, with newer interiors and a good Smart class. On Rome–Milan and Rome–Naples the two are genuinely interchangeable — book whichever is cheaper that day.

What it is like

The benchmark. Connections are timed to the minute across the whole country, so a four-leg journey to a mountain village actually works — and the trains genuinely wait for each other. It is also the most expensive network in Europe at full fare, which is why the Half Fare Card or a Swiss Travel Pass is close to mandatory for a visit of any length.

The novelty here is real: all public transport in Luxembourg, trains included, has been free nationwide since 2020, so domestic journeys need no ticket at all. Small, cheap and functional, competing with RegioJet on a handful of Czech routes and reaching a few destinations further afield. The buses and trains are sold as one network, which is convenient but means some legs of a booking are not actually a train. Fine value; just read the itinerary carefully before assuming rails all the way.

What it is like

Britain's railway is fragmented between operators, which mostly matters at the ticket office rather than on board — the trains themselves are fine and LNER's East Coast route is genuinely good. Never buy on the day if you can avoid it: advance singles are a fraction of the walk-up fare, and split-ticketing sites routinely find savings the official system will not offer you.

What it is like

A proper bed between London and Scotland, in stock refurbished in 2019 — the Club rooms with en-suite showers are the ones worth having and are priced accordingly. Classic rooms are smaller and share facilities. The Fort William portion through Rannoch Moor at dawn is the most beautiful thing on the British network, and it is the reason to choose this over a flight.

What it is like

Open-access, all-electric and refreshingly simple: one class, low fares, and London to Edinburgh in about four and a half hours. Book early and it undercuts flying comfortably once airport time is counted. There is no first class and catering is a trolley, which is exactly the trade the low fare buys.

What it is like

The Dublin–Cork line is fast and comfortable, and Dublin–Belfast is an easy cross-border run. Beyond those the network thins out quickly, and large parts of the country have no train at all — plan on buses or a car for the west. Leap cards cover commuter services around Dublin but not intercity.

Cheap, slow and aging, with journey times that make sense only if you enjoy the ride. The Bucharest–Braşov climb through the Carpathians is genuinely lovely and is the one most visitors want. Sleepers on the long routes are inexpensive and basic; delays are routine, so never plan a same-day flight connection.

What it is like

A small, tidy network and very good value. Ljubljana to Bled or to Lake Bohinj is easy and cheap, and the historic Bohinj railway through the tunnels to the Soča valley is a lovely, underused ride. Trains are simple regional stock rather than anything modern, and frequencies drop at weekends.

Slow and thinly served — for most Croatian journeys the coach is faster and more frequent, which is an honest thing to know before buying a ticket. What it is like

Athens–Thessaloniki is the one route that works well, and it is a reasonable four-and-a-half-hour journey. Services elsewhere are reduced and the network has been under intense scrutiny since the 2023 Tempi collision, with safety work continuing to affect timetables. Check current schedules close to travel rather than relying on anything published in advance.

Scenic & Heritage Trains

Europe's most famous journeys — booked for the ride itself

Glacier Express
Matterhorn Gotthard Bahn + RhB · Switzerland
Scenic
↔
Route
Zermatt ↔ St. Moritz (~8h, 291 bridges, 91 tunnels)
ℹ
Panoramic windows, year-round. Seat reservation mandatory. Passes through the Oberalp Pass (2,033m).
What it is like

Marketed as the slowest express train in the world, which is the joke and the point — around eight hours from Zermatt to St Moritz through the Oberalp Pass and the Rhine gorge, in a panoramic car with a sealed roof window. Reservation and supplement are compulsory on top of a ticket or pass. The same scenery is available on ordinary regional trains for a fraction of the price if you are willing to change twice.

Bernina Express
Rhaetian Railway (RhB) · Switzerland/Italy
Scenic
↔
Route
Chur ↔ Tirano, Italy (~4h, UNESCO World Heritage)
ℹ
Crosses the Bernina Pass (2,253m) — highest rail crossing in the Alps without a tunnel. Panoramic coaches.
What it is like

The better of the two Swiss panoramic runs, and a UNESCO World Heritage line — spirals, viaducts and a climb over the Bernina Pass to the palm trees of Tirano. The panoramic train needs a reservation and a supplement; the ordinary RhB regional service runs the same track for the base fare, with windows that open. In summer the open-air carriage is worth planning around.

Flåm Railway (Flåmsbana)
Vy / Flåm Utvikling · Norway
Scenic
↔
Route
Myrdal ↔ Flåm (~1h, 863m descent into the fjord)
ℹ
One of the steepest standard-gauge railways in the world. Connects to the Bergen Line at Myrdal. Year-round, but book ahead in summer.
What it is like

Twenty minutes of very steep, very beautiful railway, and thoroughly commercialised — it is the centrepiece of the Norway in a Nutshell package and is busy in season. The scheduled photo stop at Kjosfossen waterfall is staged, and people love it anyway. Ride it, but do not expect solitude, and book the first departure of the day if you want any.

Bergen Line (Bergensbanen)
Vy · Norway
Scenic
↔
Route
Oslo ↔ Bergen (~7h, crosses Hardangervidda plateau)
ℹ
Northern Europe's highest mainline (1,237m at Finse). Dramatic transition from mountain plateau to fjord coast. Regular Vy service — no premium required.
What it is like

The overlooked bargain: an ordinary scheduled train from Oslo to Bergen across the Hardangervidda plateau, seven hours of high, bare, snow-covered emptiness, for a normal fare. No supplement, no reservation theatre, and better scenery than several paid panoramic trains. Book a minipris fare early and sit on the right leaving Oslo.

Trenitalia Regionale · Italy
Scenic

Route
La Spezia ↔ Levanto (5 villages, ~30 min end-to-end)
ℹ
The only practical way to hop between the five villages. Buy the Cinque Terre Card for unlimited daily rides + trail access.
What it is like

A shuttle rather than a journey — a few minutes between each of the five villages, running every fifteen to twenty minutes in season. The Cinque Terre Card bundles unlimited train travel with the walking paths and is almost always the right buy. Expect to stand and expect crowds between Monterosso and Riomaggiore in summer; go early or late.
